chapters.title: Deep Learning with Python, Third Edition
chapters.overview:
This is the **front cover** of *Deep Learning with Python, Third Edition*. It shows the title in large gold letters ("DEEP LEARNING with Python"), the edition ("THIRD EDITION"), the two authors — **François Chollet** and **Matthew Watson** — and the **Manning** publisher logo. On the right is a historical costume illustration (Manning's covers traditionally feature such figures; the book explains its own cover image in "about the cover illustration", listed in the contents at printed page xxii, PDF p.24).

There is no technical content here. What the cover tells you is useful context:

- **Third edition.** According to the preface (p.18), this edition "amounts to a complete rewrite of the entire book". Code from the first (2017) or second (2021) edition will often not match: the third edition uses Keras 3, which runs on top of TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX (see "About the code", p.22).
- **Two authors.** Chollet is the creator of Keras; Watson is a core Keras maintainer at Google who has worked on Gemini (see "about the authors", p.23).

**How to use this page:** nothing to study — use it to confirm you are reading the right edition, then move on to the contents (p.7 for the brief contents, p.8 onward for the detailed contents) or straight to chapter 1 (p.25).

chapters.title: Praise for the Second Edition
chapters.overview:
This page collects **praise for the second edition** (2021) of the book — the predecessor of the third edition you are reading. Eight reviewers are quoted:

- **Martin Görner (Google):** Chollet is "a master of pedagogy", explains complex concepts "with minimal fuss, cutting through the math with practical Python code", and offers insights on architectures and training tips.
- **Sayak Paul (Carted):** an exciting introduction "with lots of real-world examples", a must-read for practitioners.
- **Edmon Begoli (Oak Ridge National Laboratory):** "The modern classic just got better."
- **Yiannis Paraskevopoulos (University of West Attica):** "Truly the bible of deep learning."
- **Raushan Jha (Microsoft):** one of the best books on deep learning with Python.
- **Viton Vitanis (Viseca Payment Services):** useful "both for the novice and the more experienced" professional.
- **Todd Cook (Appen):** "Deep learning well explained, from A to Z."
- **Kjell Jansson (GubboIT):** the book implements "the democratization of AI: 'AI to the people.'"

**What this tells the reader.** The recurring themes are (1) a **code-first** style that replaces heavy math with runnable Python, (2) **practical, real-world** examples and training advice, (3) **accessibility** for beginners alongside depth for experts, and (4) **democratization** of AI. These themes match the authors' own stated goals in the preface (p.18: "there are no difficult ideas in deep learning") and in "about this book" (p.20-21: reasonable Python proficiency and high-school math suffice).

Note: these quotes are about the *second* edition; the third edition is a complete rewrite (p.18), so specific content they refer to may have changed.

chapters.title: brief contents
chapters.overview:
The **brief contents** lists all 20 chapters with their printed start pages. In this companion, PDF page = printed page + 24 for the main text (printed page 1 is PDF p.25). Note that the roman page numbers printed on the front-matter pages themselves (this page shows "v") are 2 lower than the PDF-based numbering used here ("vii").

**The book's arc**

- **Foundations (ch. 1-7):** what deep learning is (1), the math — tensors, tensor operations, gradients, backpropagation (2), the frameworks TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX and Keras (3), first classification and regression problems (4), generalization and overfitting (5), a universal workflow for ML projects (6), and Keras in depth (7).
- **Computer vision (ch. 8-12):** image classification with ConvNets (8), architecture patterns such as residual connections (9), interpreting what ConvNets learn (10), segmentation (11) and object detection (12).
- **Sequences and language (ch. 13-16):** timeseries forecasting (13), text classification (14), language models and the Transformer (15), text generation (16).
- **Generative images (ch. 17).**
- **Practice and perspective (ch. 18-20):** best practices for the real world (18), the future of AI (19), conclusions (20).

**Chapter start pages (PDF numbering)**

- **Ch. 1** What is deep learning? — starts p.25
- **Ch. 2** The mathematical building blocks of neural networks — starts p.40
- **Ch. 3** Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras — starts p.84
- **Ch. 4** Classification and regression — starts p.128
- **Ch. 5** Fundamentals of machine learning — starts p.160
- **Ch. 6** The universal workflow of machine learning — starts p.195
- **Ch. 7** A deep dive on Keras — starts p.214
- **Ch. 8** Image classification — starts p.255
- **Ch. 9** ConvNet architecture patterns — starts p.292
- **Ch. 10** Interpreting what ConvNets learn — starts p.308
- **Ch. 11** Image segmentation — starts p.332
- **Ch. 12** Object detection — starts p.353
- **Ch. 13** Timeseries forecasting — starts p.375
- **Ch. 14** Text classification — starts p.405
- **Ch. 15** Language models and the Transformer — starts p.445
- **Ch. 16** Text generation — starts p.490
- **Ch. 17** Image generation — starts p.532

**How to use it:** chapters 1-7 build on each other and should be read in order; later chapters are more modular but assume them. "About this book" (p.21) gives the authors' own road map.

chapters.title: contents
chapters.overview:
This is the first page of the **detailed contents** (which runs PDF pp.8-16). It covers:

**Front matter** (printed roman numerals as shown in the book; PDF pages in parentheses — the book's printed roman folios are 2 lower than PDF numbering):
- preface xv (p.17)
- acknowledgments xvii (p.19)
- about this book xviii (p.20) — who should read the book, the road map (p.21), and "About the code" (p.22)
- about the authors xxi (p.23)
- about the cover illustration xxii (p.24)

**Chapter 1, What is deep learning?** — printed p. 1 (PDF p.25). Its sections (PDF pages = printed + 24):

- 1.1 Artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning — p.26
- 1.2 Artificial intelligence — p.26
- 1.3 Machine learning — p.27
- 1.4 Learning rules and representations from data — p.28
- 1.5 The “deep” in “deep learning” — p.31
- 1.6 Understanding how deep learning works, in three figures — p.32
- 1.7 What makes deep learning different — p.34
- 1.8 The age of generative AI — p.35
- 1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far — p.35
- 1.10 Beware of the short-term hype — p.36
- 1.11 Summer can turn to winter — p.38
- 1.12 The promise of AI — p.38

**Reading the structure of chapter 1.** It first defines the nested fields — AI, machine learning, deep learning (1.1-1.3) — then explains learning as finding useful **representations** of data (1.4) and what "deep" means: many successive layers of representations (1.5). Section 1.6 explains the mechanism in three figures (layers parameterized by weights, a loss function measuring error, an optimizer adjusting weights). Sections 1.7-1.9 explain why deep learning displaced earlier methods, the arrival of generative AI, and achievements so far. The chapter closes with a caution about hype, the history of "AI winters", and a longer-term optimistic outlook (1.10-1.12).

**How to use it:** the preface and "about this book" are worth reading before chapter 1 — they explain the code-first approach, prerequisites (reasonable Python, high-school math) and how to run the code (Keras on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch; Colab).

chapters.title: preface
chapters.overview:
This is the first page of the **preface**. It opens by noting the "extraordinary progress" deep learning has brought to AI: within a handful of years, computer vision and natural language processing went from *near-unusable* to *highly performant systems deployed at scale* in everyday products. The authors list how broad the impact is — medical imaging, agriculture, autonomous driving, education, disaster prevention, manufacturing — and note that digital assistants are now on nearly every consumer device.

The second paragraph pivots: despite this progress, the authors believe deep learning is **still in its early days**. AI will be "a much greater wave of disruption than anything that came before it", spreading to every problem where it is useful over *decades*, with profound global social consequences. Their response is a values statement: the only way to make this transformation beneficial for everyone is to **radically democratize access** — to put understanding of deep learning (*how it works, where it fails, and how to apply it*) in the hands of as many people as possible, including non-researchers.

The third paragraph, written in the first person by François Chollet, tells the origin of **Keras**: he wrote it in March 2015 for his own machine-learning experiments, not with democratization in mind. As newcomers entered the field and adopted Keras, accessibility became an explicit design goal. The sentence continues on PDF p.18, where the preface explains how this book continues the same mission.

**How to use this page:** read it as the book's mission statement. It explains why the book favors code and intuition over heavy notation (see PDF p.20) and why Keras is the main tool throughout (introduced technically on PDF p.114).

chapters.title: acknowledgments
chapters.overview:
The **acknowledgments** page thanks the people behind the book.

- **The Keras community** comes first: over the past decade Keras has grown to **thousands of open-source contributors** and **more than 2 million users**, whose contributions and feedback made Keras what it is.
- **Personal thanks**: François Chollet thanks his wife for her support during the development of Keras and the writing of the book; Matthew Watson thanks his partner Kate, his family and friends.
- **Manning**: publisher Marjan Bace and the editorial and production teams, including Michael Stephens and Aleksandar Dragosavljević.
- **Peer reviewers**: a long list of named reviewers (Aakash Nain, Abheesht Sharma, Margaret Maynard-Reid, Todd Cook, Varun Chawla and many others) plus everyone who sent feedback on the draft.
- **Coding side**: Tomasz Kalinowski contributed to the code examples, Ian Hough was the development editor, and Gabriel Rasskin was the technical proofreader.

**How to use this page:** there is nothing to study here, but two points are worth remembering. Keras is a large, community-driven open-source project (useful context for chapter 3, PDF p.114, and chapter 7, PDF p.215), and the book's code was reviewed by a technical proofreader, which is a good reason to run the listings as written before modifying them.

chapters.title: about this book
chapters.overview:
This page opens **about this book**.

**Audience in one line.** The book is for anyone who wants to explore deep learning *from scratch* or broaden their understanding — practicing ML engineers, software developers and college students alike.

**Teaching approach.** You start simply and work up to **state-of-the-art techniques**. The authors aim for a balance of **intuition, theory and hands-on practice**. The book **avoids mathematical notation**: core ideas are explained through **functioning code paired with explanations of the underlying principles**. You will train models from scratch in several problem domains and learn practical recommendations for writing deep learning programs and **deploying them in the real world**.

**Promised outcomes.** After the book you should:

1. understand *what deep learning is*, *when it is applicable*, and *what its limitations are*;
2. know the **standard workflow** for approaching and solving machine learning problems (chapter 6, "the universal workflow of machine learning");
3. know how to address commonly encountered issues.

**Who should read this book.** The primary reader has *some Python programming experience* and wants to get started with machine learning and deep learning. The list of other readers begins here: a **data scientist** familiar with machine learning will get a solid, practical introduction to deep learning, which the authors call "the fastest-growing and most significant subfield of machine learning". The list continues on PDF p.21 (Keras newcomers, graduate students, non-coders) along with the prerequisites (reasonable Python, high-school math).

**How to use this page:** keep the three outcomes as a checklist; at the end of the book (chapter 20's review, PDF p.621) check whether you can explain each.

chapters.title: about the authors
chapters.overview:
This page gives two short author biographies, each next to a portrait photo.

**François Chollet** has worked with deep learning since it began gaining traction in academia in **2012**. He is the author of **Keras**, one of the most popular deep learning libraries, used in university classrooms, at companies such as Google, Netflix and Spotify, and in scientific organizations such as CERN and NASA. He co-founded the **Ndea** research lab for frontier AI systems and created the **ARC-AGI** challenge for measuring machine intelligence.

**Matthew Watson** has worked on machine learning at Google since **2018**, including on the **Gemini** model and Google's open-source deep learning ecosystem. He is a **core maintainer of Keras**, focusing on its **natural language processing** tools. He holds a master's in computer science from **Stanford**, where he researched procedural modeling techniques at the Stanford Graphics Lab.

**How to use this page:** the bios hint at where each author's expertise shows in the book. Chollet's work on Keras underpins chapters 3 and 7, and his ARC-AGI work is the basis for the discussion of intelligence, the ARC Prize and test-time adaptation in chapter 19 (PDF p.600–607 per the contents). Watson's NLP focus aligns with the text and generative chapters (14–16).

chapters.title: about the cover illustration
chapters.overview:
The last front-matter page explains the **cover illustration**. The figure is captioned **"Habit of a Persian Lady in 1568"** and comes from **Thomas Jefferys'** *A Collection of the Dresses of Different Nations, Ancient and Modern*, published between **1757 and 1772**.

The second paragraph explains Manning's reasoning: in earlier centuries, a person's region and trade or station in life could be identified from their dress. Manning "celebrates the inventiveness and initiative of the computer business" with covers based on the rich regional diversity of centuries ago, brought back to life by pictures from such collections.

**How to use this page:** there is nothing to study here. The book proper starts on the next page with chapter 1, *What is deep learning?* (PDF p.25).

chapters.title: 1 What is deep learning?
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **Chapter 1, "What is deep learning?"**. It is a chapter opener: a large chapter number, the title, a "This chapter covers" box, and the first paragraph of the chapter.

The box lists three things the chapter will do:

- give **high-level definitions of fundamental concepts** (AI, machine learning, deep learning — developed in sections 1.1–1.6, p.26–34),
- offer **a soft introduction to the principles behind machine learning** (how a model learns rules and representations from data, p.28–34),
- discuss **deep learning's rising popularity and future potential** (sections 1.7–1.12, p.34–39).

The opening paragraph starts from the media hype of the past decade. AI, machine learning and deep learning appear in countless articles, often in non-technical outlets, promising intelligent chatbots, self-driving cars and virtual assistants — a future painted sometimes as grim, sometimes as utopian, with scarce human jobs and most economic activity handled by robots or AI agents. The authors' point is practical: a machine learning practitioner must be able to **recognize the signal amid the noise**, telling world-changing developments from overhyped press releases. They add a motivating note — "our future is at stake" and you have an active role, because after reading the book you will be among those who can actually build these systems. The sentence breaks off with "So let's" and continues on p.26 with the questions the chapter will tackle: what deep learning has achieved so far, how significant it is, where we are headed, and whether to believe the hype.

How to use this page: read the bullet box as a map of the chapter, then keep the "signal amid the noise" theme in mind — it returns explicitly in section 1.10, *Beware of the short-term hype* (p.36), and section 1.11, *Summer can turn to winter* (p.38), and again in the book's closing reflections (p.621).

chapters.title: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 2, *The mathematical building blocks of neural networks*** (PDF p.40–83). The 'This chapter covers' box lists three topics: a first example of a neural network; tensors and tensor operations; and how neural networks learn via backpropagation and gradient descent.

The two introductory paragraphs set out the approach. Understanding deep learning requires familiarity with many *simple* mathematical concepts — tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent and so on — and the chapter's goal is to build intuition for them without getting overly technical. The authors deliberately steer away from mathematical notation, which can be an unnecessary barrier for readers without a mathematics background and is not needed to explain things well; in their words, 'the most precise, unambiguous description of a mathematical operation is its executable code.'

The plan: to give context for tensors and gradient descent, the chapter begins with a practical neural-network example (section 2.1, p.41 — classifying handwritten digits with Keras), then goes over every new concept point by point: data representations / tensors (2.2, p.45), tensor operations (2.3, p.52), gradient-based optimization including derivatives, SGD and backpropagation (2.4, p.63), and finally a from-scratch reimplementation of the first example (2.5, p.75). The authors stress that these concepts are essential for understanding the practical examples in the following chapters. The next page (p.41) adds a note on running the book's code in Jupyter notebooks and Google Colab.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. The bullets correspond to sections 2.1, 2.2–2.3, and 2.4–2.5 respectively; the concept list in the first paragraph (tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent) is the vocabulary you should be able to explain by the chapter's end.

chapters.title: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 3, "Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras"** (PDF pp.84-127).

The *This chapter covers* box lists two goals:

- a closer look at all major deep learning frameworks and their relationships;
- an overview of how core deep learning concepts translate to code across all frameworks.

The introduction says the chapter is meant to give you everything you need to start doing deep learning in practice. First you get familiar with three popular frameworks that can be used with Keras: **TensorFlow** (tensorflow.org), **PyTorch** (pytorch.org) and **JAX** (jax.readthedocs.io). Then, building on the first contact with Keras in chapter 2, the chapter reviews the core components of neural networks and how they translate to Keras APIs. By the end you should be ready for practical, real-world applications, which start in chapter 4.

According to the chapter outline, the sections are: 3.1 a brief history of deep learning frameworks (p.85); 3.2 how these frameworks relate to each other (p.87); 3.3 TensorFlow, 3.4 PyTorch and 3.5 JAX, each with first steps, an end-to-end linear classifier written in that framework alone, and what makes its approach unique (pp.87-114); and 3.6 Keras (p.114), covering layers, models, the compile step, loss functions, fit(), validation monitoring and inference.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a map. If you already know one framework, the parallel structure of sections 3.3-3.5 (the same linear classifier in each) makes them easy to compare side by side.

chapters.title: 4 Classification and regression
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 4, "Classification and regression"** (PDF pages 128-159).

**This chapter covers:** your first examples of real-world machine learning workflows; handling binary and categorical classification problems; handling continuous regression problems.

The introduction says the chapter will consolidate what you learned in chapters 2 and 3 by applying it to three tasks that span the **three most common use cases** of neural networks:

- **Binary classification:** classifying movie reviews as positive or negative (section 4.1, IMDb, p.130).
- **Categorical (multiclass) classification:** classifying newswires by topic (section 4.2, Reuters, p.140).
- **Scalar regression:** estimating the price of a house from real-estate data (section 4.3, California Housing Price dataset, p.150).

These examples are your first contact with **end-to-end workflows**: data preprocessing, basic model architecture principles and model evaluation. Use this page as a roadmap: each section follows the same pattern (dataset, preparing the data, building the model, validating the approach, generating predictions, wrapping up), so you can compare how each choice changes with the problem type.

chapters.title: 5 Fundamentals of machine learning
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 5, "Fundamentals of machine learning"** (PDF pp.160-194). The *This chapter covers* box lists four themes:

- **The tension between generalization and optimization**, called *the fundamental issue in machine learning* (section 5.1, p.160).
- **Evaluation methods** for machine learning models (section 5.2, p.173: training/validation/test sets, common-sense baselines).
- **Best practices to improve model fitting** (section 5.3, p.177: tuning gradient-descent parameters, better architecture priors, more capacity).
- **Best practices to achieve better generalization** (section 5.4, p.182: dataset curation, feature engineering, early stopping, regularization).

The introductory paragraph links back to chapter 4. After the IMDb, Reuters and housing examples you should be comfortable with classification and regression, and you have *witnessed the central problem of machine learning: overfitting*. Chapter 5 will **formalize** that intuition into a solid conceptual framework, stressing **accurate model evaluation** and the **balance between training and generalization**.

Section **5.1, "Generalization: The goal of machine learning"**, begins at the bottom of the page. It recalls that all three chapter 4 examples split the data into training, validation and test sets. The sentence continues on p.161, which explains why: performance on unseen data diverges from training performance after a few epochs.

*How to use this page:* treat the four bullets as a map of the chapter (see the diagram) and keep the chapter 4 examples in mind as concrete cases of each idea.

chapters.title: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 6, "The universal workflow of machine learning."**

**This chapter covers:**
- Framing a machine learning problem
- Developing a working model
- Deploying your model in production and maintaining it

The opening text points out that all previous examples assumed a labeled dataset already existed, so training could start immediately. In the real world, "you don't start from a dataset; you start from a problem."

To make this concrete, the authors ask you to imagine launching your own ML consulting shop. Projects start rolling in; the first two on this page are:
- a **personalized photo search engine** for a picture-sharing social network (type "wedding" and retrieve your wedding pictures with no manual tagging), and
- **flagging spam and offensive text** in the posts of a budding chat app.

The list continues on p.196 (music recommendation, credit card fraud, ad click-through rate, anomalous cookies on a production line, archaeological sites from satellite images), followed by the three-part structure of the workflow: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.

**How to use this page:** treat the chapter map below as your roadmap; as you read each project, ask yourself what the input data, target, and success metric would be — that is exactly what section 6.1 teaches.

chapters.title: 7 A deep dive on Keras
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **Chapter 7, "A deep dive on Keras"** (PDF pp. 214–254). The "This chapter covers" box lists five topics:

- **The different ways to create Keras models**: the `Sequential` class, the **Functional API**, and **model subclassing** (section 7.2, from p.216).
- **The built-in Keras training and evaluation loops**, including **custom metrics and custom losses** (section 7.3, from p.230).
- **Keras callbacks** to further customize how training proceeds (p.232–p.234).
- **TensorBoard** for monitoring training and evaluation metrics over time (p.236).
- **Writing your own training and evaluation loops from scratch** (section 7.4, from p.238).

The introductory paragraph recaps what the reader already knows: the Sequential model, `Dense` layers, and the built-in APIs for training, evaluation and inference (`compile()`, `fit()`, `evaluate()`, `predict()`). In chapter 3 the reader also learned to inherit from the `Layer` class to create custom layers. The sentence continues on p.215, which mentions using the gradient APIs of TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch for a step-by-step training loop, and explains that later applications need much more than `Sequential` and the default `fit()`.

**How to use this page:** treat the bullet list as a roadmap. The chapter follows Keras's principle of *progressive disclosure of complexity* (p.215): each section adds flexibility on top of the previous one. You will get the most from it if you are comfortable with `fit()` and custom `Layer` subclasses.

chapters.title: 8 Image classification
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 8, Image classification**. The box *This chapter covers* lists four topics:

- Understanding convolutional neural networks (**ConvNets**)
- Using **data augmentation** to mitigate overfitting
- Using a **pretrained ConvNet for feature extraction**
- **Fine-tuning** a pretrained ConvNet

The introduction sets the historical scene. Computer vision was *the first big success story of deep learning* and drove its initial rise between 2011 and 2015. Convolutional neural networks began getting remarkably good results on image classification competitions: first **Dan Ciresan** won two niche competitions (the **ICDAR 2011** Chinese character recognition competition and the **IJCNN 2011** German traffic signs recognition competition), and then, more notably, in fall **2012** **Hinton's group** won the high-profile **ImageNet** large-scale visual recognition challenge. Many more promising results followed in other vision tasks.

The second paragraph begins a twist: these early successes *weren't quite enough to make deep learning mainstream at the time; it took a few years*. The sentence continues on p.256, which describes the skepticism of the computer vision community until 2016.

How to use this page: treat the bullet list as the chapter roadmap. Section 8.1 (p.256) introduces ConvNets with an MNIST example and explains convolution (p.258) and max pooling (p.263); 8.2 (p.265) trains a ConvNet from scratch on a small dataset and introduces data augmentation (p.276); 8.3 (p.280) covers feature extraction and fine-tuning with a pretrained model.

chapters.title: 9 ConvNet architecture patterns
chapters.overview:
This is the **opening page of chapter 9, "ConvNet architecture patterns."** The box *This chapter covers* lists three topics:

- **The modularity-hierarchy-reuse formula** for model architecture (section 9.1, p.293).
- **Standard best practices for building ConvNets**: **residual connections** (9.2, p.296), **batch normalization** (9.3, p.300) and **depthwise separable convolutions** (9.4, p.302), combined in a mini Xception-like model (9.5, p.304).
- **Ongoing design trends** for computer vision models, including Vision Transformers (9.6, p.306).

The first paragraph defines a model's **architecture** as the sum of the choices that went into creating it: which layers to use, how to configure them, and in what arrangement to connect them. These choices define the model's **hypothesis space**: the space of possible functions that gradient descent can search over, parameterized by the model's weights. Like feature engineering, a good hypothesis space encodes **prior knowledge** about the problem and its solution. For example, using convolution layers means you know in advance that the relevant patterns in your input images are translation-invariant (the sentence finishes on p.293).

**How to use this page:** read it as a map. If you used Xception in chapter 8 without knowing why it looks the way it does, this chapter explains its ingredients one by one.

chapters.title: 10 Interpreting what ConvNets learn
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 10, "Interpreting what ConvNets learn"** (PDF pp.308–331). The box **This chapter covers** lists three topics:

- interpreting how ConvNets **decompose an input image** (intermediate activations, section 10.1, p.309),
- **visualizing the filters** learned by ConvNets (section 10.2, p.315),
- visualizing the **areas of an image responsible for a classification decision** (class activation heatmaps, section 10.3, p.323).

The chapter outline also includes section 10.4, visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet (p.330).

The first paragraph frames the problem of **interpretability**: *why* did your classifier think an image contained a fridge when all you can see is a truck? This matters most when deep learning **complements human expertise**, as in **medical imaging**, where a prediction alone is not enough and practitioners need to see what drove it. The chapter introduces a range of techniques for visualizing what ConvNets learn and understanding their decisions.

The second paragraph addresses the common claim that deep learning models are **"black boxes"** whose representations are hard to extract and present in human-readable form. The authors grant that this is partly true for some models, but **definitely not for ConvNets**: their representations are highly amenable to visualization, largely because they are **representations of visual concepts**. The sentence beginning "Since 2013, a…" continues on p.309, which lists the techniques the chapter will cover.

Use this page as a map for the chapter. Sections 10.2 and 10.3 come in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX versions (pp.318–319, 326–327).

chapters.title: 11 Image segmentation
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 11, Image segmentation**. The "This chapter covers" box lists three topics:

- the different branches of computer vision: **image classification, image segmentation, and object detection**;
- **building a segmentation model from scratch** (section 11.2, from p.335);
- **using the pretrained Segment Anything Model** (section 11.3, from p.342).

The introduction recalls that chapter 8 introduced deep learning for vision through a simple use case, *binary image classification*, and says computer vision is more than that. This chapter goes deeper into another essential application, image segmentation.

Section **11.1 Computer vision tasks** begins by summarizing what classification does: "an image goes in, a label comes out" ("this image likely contains a cat; this other one likely contains a dog"). It then states that there are three essential computer vision tasks to know about. The list itself (classification, segmentation, detection, with figure 11.1) continues on p.333.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a roadmap. The chapter first sets out the task landscape and the types of segmentation (semantic, instance, panoptic; p.334), then trains a small segmentation model on a downloaded dataset, and finally shows how to prompt SAM with points and boxes. Object detection, mentioned in the first bullet, is covered in detail in chapter 12 (p.334, p.354).

chapters.title: 12 Object detection
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 12, Object detection**. The "This chapter covers" box lists four topics:

- understanding the object detection problem,
- two-stage and single-stage object detectors,
- training a simple single-stage detector from scratch,
- using a pretrained object detector.

The opening paragraph defines the task: object detection is "all about drawing boxes (called *bounding boxes*) around objects of interest in a picture" (see Figure 12.1, printed on p.354). Detection tells you **which** objects are present and **where** they are. Three common applications follow:

- **Counting**: how many instances of an object are in an image;
- **Tracking**: following how objects move in a scene by running detection on every frame of a movie;
- **Cropping**: locating the region containing an object of interest so that a higher-resolution patch can be sent to a classifier or an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. According to the chapter outline, section 12.1 (p.354) contrasts two-stage R-CNN detectors with single-stage detectors, 12.2 (p.356) trains a YOLO model from scratch on COCO, and 12.3 (p.370) uses a pretrained RetinaNet. The page connects directly to chapter 11: the box prompts used with SAM on p.351-352 are exactly the kind of bounding box a detector outputs, and p.354 will argue that segmentation is a strict superset of detection but much costlier to run and to label.

chapters.title: 13 Timeseries forecasting
chapters.overview:
This is the **opening page of chapter 13, Timeseries forecasting**. The 'This chapter covers' box lists three topics:

- an overview of **machine learning for timeseries**;
- understanding **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)**;
- applying RNNs to a **temperature forecasting example**.

The introduction says the chapter tackles timeseries, 'where temporal order is everything', and focuses on the most common and valuable timeseries task, **forecasting**: using the recent past to predict the near future, e.g. to anticipate energy demand, manage inventory or forecast the weather.

**Section 13.1, Different kinds of timeseries tasks**, begins by defining a *timeseries* as any data obtained via **measurements at regular intervals** — the daily price of a stock, a city's hourly electricity consumption, a store's weekly sales. Timeseries appear in natural phenomena (seismic activity, fish populations in a river, the weather at a location) and in human activity (website visitors, a country's GDP, credit card transactions). The final sentence, 'Unlike the types of data you’ve encountered so far,' continues on p.376, where the authors explain that working with timeseries means understanding a system's *dynamics*.

How to use this page: treat it as a roadmap. The chapter builds the Jena weather dataset (p.376–382), sets a commonsense baseline (p.383), tries dense and 1D-convolutional models (p.384–387), and then develops RNNs, recurrent dropout, stacking and bidirectional RNNs (p.388–402).

chapters.title: 14 Text classification
chapters.overview:
This is the **opening page of chapter 14, "Text classification."** The "This chapter covers" box lists three topics:

- An introduction to the field of **natural language processing (NLP)**
- **Preprocessing text input into numeric input**
- **Building simple text classification models**

The introductory paragraph says this chapter lays the foundation for working with text that the *next two chapters* build on (chapter 15, "Language models and the Transformer", and chapter 16, "Text generation"). By the end, you will be able to build a simple text classifier in several different ways, which sets up more complex models such as the Transformer in chapter 15.

Section **14.1, "A brief history of natural language processing,"** then begins. In computer science, human languages such as English or Mandarin are called "natural" to distinguish them from languages designed for machines, such as LISP, Assembly and XML. Every machine language was *designed*: an engineer first wrote down formal rules for which statements are valid and what they mean, and people used the language only once the rules were complete. The sentence "With human language," breaks off at the page end and continues on p.406: *"it's the reverse: usage comes first, and rules arise later."*

**How to use this page:** read it as a roadmap. The chapter outline runs from history (p.405), to text preparation and tokenization (p.408-p.418), to sets versus sequences and the IMDb dataset (p.419-p.421), to set models such as bag-of-words and bigrams (p.422-p.428), and finally to sequence models (RNNs and word embeddings, p.429-p.444).

chapters.title: 15 Language models and the Transformer
chapters.overview:
This is the **opening page of Chapter 15, *Language models and the Transformer***. The "This chapter covers" box lists three goals:

- **How to generate text with a deep learning model.** Section 15.1 builds a character-level Shakespeare language model (p.446-452).
- **Training a model to translate from English to Spanish.** Section 15.2 frames translation as sequence-to-sequence learning, first with RNNs (p.452-460).
- **The Transformer, a powerful architecture for text modeling problems.** Section 15.3 covers dot-product attention, encoder and decoder blocks, and positional embeddings (p.461-477). Section 15.4 then fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer encoder on IMDb (p.478-484), and section 15.5 asks what makes the Transformer effective (p.485).

The introductory paragraph says the chapter builds on Chapter 14's preprocessing basics to tackle "more involved language problems such as machine translation," and to build intuition for the Transformer, which "powers products like ChatGPT."

Section **15.1 The language model** begins at the bottom of the page. Chapter 14 converted text to numbers to classify reviews, but classification is "a uniquely simple problem": the output is a single float for binary classification, or at worst N numbers for N-way classification. The next page (p.446) shows why generating text is harder. The space of possible output sequences is astronomically large, so the practical approach is a model that predicts one token at a time, $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a roadmap. The pretraining idea from the end of Chapter 14 (p.444) reappears here at scale, since language modeling is the unsupervised task that Transformers are pretrained on.

chapters.title: 16 Text generation
chapters.overview:
This is the **opening page of chapter 16, *Text generation***. The "This chapter covers" box lists four goals:

- **A brief history of generative modeling**: section 16.1 (p.492) traces sequence generation from early models to GPT.
- **Training a miniature GPT model from scratch**: section 16.2 (p.494) pretrains a decoder-only Transformer on part of the C4 corpus, then explores generative decoding and sampling strategies (pp.502-507).
- **Using a pretrained Transformer model to build a chatbot**: section 16.3 (p.508) generates text with the Gemma model, then covers instruction fine-tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
- **Building a multimodal model that can describe images in natural language**: part of section 16.4 (Multimodal LLMs, p.522), alongside RLHF, retrieval-augmented generation and "reasoning" models. Section 16.5 (p.528) asks where LLMs are heading.

The introduction opens with a first-person recollection (François Chollet's voice): in **2014**, his claim that most of the cultural content we consume would soon be created with substantial help from AI met with "utter disbelief", even among long-time ML practitioners. A decade later that disbelief has largely receded. Generative tools are built into word processors, image editors and development environments, and prestigious awards have gone to AI-assisted art and literature, "to considerable controversy and debate". **Footnote 1** gives the examples: Jason Allen won a digital-art award in 2022 with an image made in Midjourney, and in 2024 Rie Kudan won one of Japan's most prestigious literary awards for a novel written with substantial help from generative software. The sentence continues on p.491, where the authors argue for AI as *augmented* rather than artificial intelligence.

chapters.title: 17 Image generation
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 17, Image generation**. The 'This chapter covers' box lists four topics: **variational autoencoders**, **diffusion models**, **using a pretrained text-to-image model**, and **exploring the latent image spaces learned by text-to-image models**.

The opening paragraph calls image generation the most popular and successful application of creative AI today, and defines it compactly: *learning latent visual spaces and sampling from them* to create new pictures *interpolated from real ones* — imaginary people, places, cats and dogs.

Section **17.1, Deep learning for image generation**, then begins: this section and the next review high-level concepts and implementation details of the two main techniques, VAEs and diffusion models. The authors add (the sentence finishes on p.533) that these techniques are not specific to images — the same ideas could be used for sound or music — but images have produced the most interesting results so far.

How to use this page: treat it as the map for the chapter. VAEs are covered in 17.1.2–17.1.3 (p.534–541), diffusion models in 17.2 (p.542–554), and text-to-image models in 17.3 (p.555 onward).

chapters.title: 18 Best practices for the real world
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of **chapter 18, "Best practices for the real world."** The *This chapter covers* box lists five topics: **hyperparameter tuning**, **model ensembling**, **training Keras models on multiple GPUs or on TPU**, **mixed-precision training**, and **quantization**.

The introduction first takes stock. You can now train image classification and segmentation models, classification or regression models on vector data, timeseries forecasting models, text classification models, sequence-to-sequence models, and generative models for text and images. In the authors' words, "you've got all the bases covered."

Then comes the caveat. Every model so far was trained **at small scale**, on small datasets with a single GPU, and generally did **not reach the best achievable performance** on its dataset. The book is introductory, so to reach state-of-the-art results on brand-new problems there is "still a bit of a chasm" to cross. The chapter (continuing on p.563) is about bridging it.

**How to use this page:** treat the five bullets as a roadmap. The first two (tuning, ensembling) are about getting the most accuracy out of a model and make up section 18.1, starting on p.563. The last three are about compute: scaling training across devices (18.2, p.572) and using lower-precision numbers to speed up training and inference (18.3, p.580).

chapters.title: 19 The future of AI
chapters.overview:
This is the opening page of chapter 19, **The future of AI**. The "This chapter covers" box lists four themes: the limitations of deep learning; the nature of intelligence; what's missing from current approaches; and what the future might look like.

The introduction argues that using a tool appropriately requires understanding not only what it *can* do but also what it *can't*. The author will first give an overview of key limitations of deep learning and then offer *speculative* thoughts on the future evolution of AI and what it would take to reach human-level general intelligence, which he says should be especially interesting for readers who want to get into fundamental research.

Section **19.1 The limitations of deep learning** begins: there are infinitely many things deep learning can do, but it can't do *everything*; you should know its limitations, not just its strengths. "So where does deep learning fall short?" The answers start on p.589.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. Sections 19.1 (limitations: novelty, sensitivity to phrasing, failing to learn generalizable programs, anthropomorphizing), 19.2 (scale isn't all you need), 19.3 (how to build intelligence, including the kaleidoscope hypothesis and the ARC Prize) and 19.4 (search, symbols and program synthesis) correspond roughly to the four bullets. Note that the chapter explicitly mixes established observations with the author's own speculation.

chapters.title: 20 Conclusions
chapters.overview:
This page opens **chapter 20, Conclusions**. The "This chapter covers" box lists two topics: **important takeaways from this book** and **resources for learning further and applying your skills in practice**.

The introduction says the chapter will start with a **bird's-eye view** of what you should take away from the book, to refresh your memory of key concepts, and then give a short list of **resources and strategies** for learning more about machine learning and keeping up with new advances. It stresses that becoming an effective AI practitioner is a **journey**, and finishing the book is merely the **first step**; the aim is to equip you to continue on your own.

**Section 20.1, Key concepts in review**, begins here: it briefly synthesizes the book's key takeaways and is meant to be reread as a **quick refresher**. Based on the chapter outline, 20.1 covers approaches to AI, what makes deep learning special, how to think about deep learning, key enabling technologies, the universal ML workflow and key network architectures (pp.620-628); then come 20.2 Limitations of deep learning (p.629), 20.3 What might lie ahead (p.630), 20.4 Staying up to date (Kaggle, arXiv, the Keras ecosystem, pp.631-632) and 20.5 Final words (p.632).

chapters.title: index
chapters.overview:
This is the **first page of the index** (printed page 609, PDF 633). It opens with the large *index* title and covers the letter **A**, from *abstraction acquisition* to *axis_names argument*.

**How to use it.** Index entries cite **printed** page numbers. To find the page in this PDF companion, **add 24** (for example, printed 464 becomes PDF 488). Indented lines are sub-entries of the heading above them, and a range such as 576–584 means a continuous discussion.

**What clusters here.**
- **AI and AGI, the big picture.** *AI (artificial intelligence)* 2 (PDF 26) has many sub-entries: AI winters 14 (PDF 38), building intelligence 576–584 (PDF 600–608), local vs. extreme generalization 573 (PDF 597), search and symbols 584–594 (PDF 608–618), and future developments 606 (PDF 630). Related entries are *AGI* 13, 571, 594 (PDF 37, 595, 618), *ARC-AGI* 581, 583 (PDF 605, 607), *ARC Prize* 581, *abstraction acquisition* 578 (PDF 602), *automatons* 571 and *AI summer* 597.
- **Attention.** *attention* 464 (PDF 488), with *dot-product attention* 439 (PDF 463) and *Transformer architecture* 437 (PDF 461). *attention_mask* is at 446–447 (PDF 470–471).
- **Optimizers.** *adam optimizer* 247, 379, 490 (PDF 271, 403, 514) and *AdamW optimizer* 529 (PDF 553).
- **Models and techniques.** *autoencoders* 510 (PDF 534), *autoregressive model* 426 (PDF 450), *activation functions* 109 (PDF 133), *adversarial examples* 567 (PDF 591), *anomaly detection* 352 (PDF 376), *augmenting text data* 413.
- **Keras API names.** *adapt()* 399, *add()* 192, *append()* 192, *axis_names argument* 553 (distribution API).
